paragraphs.heading: Size and direction
paragraphs.text: Velocity measures speed in a particular direction of motion. That makes it a vector quantity: both a size, called its magnitude, and a direction are needed to define it. Strip away the direction and the magnitude left over is speed, measured in metres per second in the SI system.

paragraphs.heading: Scalar or vector
paragraphs.text: A simple example shows the difference. "5 metres per second" is a scalar, while "5 metres per second east" is a vector. Everyday speech often treats speed and velocity as the same, but in physics speed tells only how fast, while velocity adds the direction.

paragraphs.heading: Turning counts as accelerating
paragraphs.text: Because velocity carries direction, a change of direction is a change of velocity. Any change in speed, direction or both is called acceleration. Constant velocity needs a steady speed in a fixed direction, which means straight-line motion. A car going round a circle at a constant 20 kilometres per hour has a steady speed but a changing velocity, so it is accelerating.

paragraphs.heading: Subtracting vectors
paragraphs.text: Treating velocity as a vector makes it easy to compare two moving objects. If object A has velocity vector v and object B has velocity vector w, both given in the same inertial reference frame, then A's velocity relative to B is v − w. B's velocity relative to A is w − v. In one dimension the velocities become scalars: v_rel = v − (−w) when the objects head in opposite directions, and v_rel = v − (+ w) when they head the same way.

paragraphs.heading: Writing the parts
paragraphs.text: A velocity vector can be broken into Cartesian components, one along each of the x-, y- and z-axes. Some textbooks label these components with subscripts. Others name them u, v and w.

paragraphs.heading: Quantities built on it
paragraphs.text: Several other quantities are built from velocity. Momentum, p, is mass times velocity, 𝒑 = m𝒗, and is a vector. Kinetic energy, Eₖ = 1/2mv², is a scalar, since it depends on the square of the velocity. Leaving Earth from its surface takes an escape velocity of about 11 200 m/s, whichever way the object heads, so it is really a speed, and "escape speed" would be the better name.
